source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"CA-125 is associated with ovarian cancer, but benign conditions and other malignancies can also elevate it, so the result is not diagnostic by itself.","B":"CA-125 is specific for lung cancer, so an elevated result makes an ovarian or other gynecologic source unlikely in a client with a pelvic mass.","C":"CA-125 has no recognized association with ovarian cancer and is not used as a tumor marker in evaluating or monitoring ovarian malignancy.","D":"CA-125 is specific for prostate disease, so an elevated result should be interpreted mainly as evidence of prostate pathology rather than a pelvic mass."}}
source_row.rationale: CA-125 is a tumor-associated marker commonly linked with ovarian cancer, but it lacks sufficient specificity to diagnose ovarian cancer by itself because benign conditions and other cancers can also elevate it. Option A is correct. Options B and D assign CA-125 to unrelated primary disease categories. Option C incorrectly denies its established ovarian-cancer association.
source_row.source_detail: National Cancer Institute — Ovarian Cancer Screening (PDQ), CA-125: CA-125 is associated with ovarian cancer but lacks diagnostic specificity; elevated values can occur in benign gynecologic/non-gynecologic conditions and other malignancies, so the result cannot diagnose ovarian cancer by itself. Current NCI Ovarian Cancer Screening PDQ live-rechecked 2026-08-15; difficulty corrected to easy because the item tests direct nonspecific-marker interpretation. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: diagnostic probability tools, laboratory/tumor-marker interpretation, ECG/lab monitoring and potential complications. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: A client being evaluated for a pelvic mass has an elevated CA-125 level and asks whether this confirms ovarian cancer. Which response is most accurate?
